CHIEF COMPLAINT
Nonhealing foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male with diabetes who presents with a nonhealing foot ulcer on the right foot that has been present for approximately 2 months. Patient reports that the ulcer recently became red and started draining, which prompted him to seek care. He recalls the injury occurred from walking barefoot at Dewey Beach. Patient denies severe pain but describes an occasional throbbing sensation and increased pressure sensation at the site. His primary concern is the new onset drainage and redness. Patient's PCP previously initiated antibiotic therapy, but the patient has not yet filled the prescription. Patient is uncertain of the specific antibiotic name. Regarding his diabetes, patient reports taking his medication but does not check his blood sugar regularly. He reports his last A1C was approximately 10.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient denies fever. Denies severe localized pain. Describes occasional throbbing at ulcer site. No other systemic symptoms elicited.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Diabetes mellitus.

MEDICATIONS
Diabetes medication (specific agent not documented).

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as an ambulance driver. Engages in barefoot activities on beaches.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Normal, no fever. Right foot examination reveals a 1 x 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, proximal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. Noted erythema, drainage, and edema surrounding the wound. Fluid expressed from the wound. No evidence of necrotic tissue, odor, or bony exposure. Palpation elicits increased pressure sensation without sharp pain. Clinical assessment suggests infection is present.

RESULTS
X-ray of right foot: No evidence of osteomyelitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diabetic foot ulcer with infection. Plan includes: (1) Order ankle-brachial index (ABI) to assess blood supply to the foot; (2) Perform debridement of wound to remove dead tissue; (3) Prescribe clindamycin 400 mg orally twice daily for 7 days to treat infection; (4) Dispense surgical shoe for patient to wear for the next month to reduce pressure on the foot and promote healing; (5) Follow-up appointment in 2 weeks with possible repeat debridement; (6) Patient to call office if any issues arise between visits; (7) Patient instructed to seek urgent care or emergency department if fever or emergency symptoms develop. Patient counseled to follow up with primary care physician to optimize diabetic control, as current A1C of approximately 10 is suboptimal.
